corr.head: StressTyp2's coding does not match the source
corr.detail: Under every reading, the fifth syllable of a five-syllable word is unstressed: the database's own quoted passage from Hayes, Tryon (who gives secondary stress on the third syllable only), and instrumental work (which finds no word stress at all). Dehu therefore leaves the Maranungku-type pattern class.

contra.head: Later instrumental work finds no word stress
contra.detail: StressTyp2 codes a word-level pattern (10 101 1010 10100 101000 1010000 10100000), a rule Tryon 1968 states for the word alone (stress 'indicates the division between words'; intonation is treated separately in 1.3). Torres & Fletcher 2022 find no acoustic evidence for word-initial primary or third-syllable secondary stress and analyse Drehu prominence as post-lexical right-edge marking which could be phrasal, so the record is classed as a conflict between sources, not as a fixed pattern.

88.prule: Primary stress always on the first syllable of the word; non-phonemic, demarcative of word boundaries; each element of a compound or reduplicative carries its own primary stress (Tryon 1968). Torres & Fletcher 2022 find no acoustic evidence for word-initial prominence.
88.srule: One secondary stress, always on the third syllable of polysyllabic words (final in trisyllables, penult in four-syllable words, antepenult in five-syllable words); non-iterating, all other non-initial syllables unstressed. Contested: Torres & Fletcher 2022 (Glossa 7(1), p. 5) report no acoustic evidence for the third-syllable secondary (or the initial primary) and analyse Drehu as right-edge phrasal marking.

morph.src: Tryon, D.T. 1968 [1967]. Dehu Grammar. Pacific Linguistics Series B, No. 7. Canberra: ANU. xii+122 pp. DOI 10.15144/PL-B7 (CC BY-SA 4.0 online edition). Full scan in the copy consulted; interlinear texts in Appendix pp. 99-110, Word Level Analysis ch. 4 pp. 94-98, Phrase Level ch. 3 pp. 46-93, Phonology ch. 1 pp. 1-14.
morph.rootq: §1.1 p.1: 'In Dehu stress is non-phonemic, having only a demarkative function. It indicates the division between words. ... (a) Primary Stress: Primary stress always falls on the first syllable of the word. With compound words, both elements have a primary stress, this being true also of reduplicatives. (b) Secondary Stress: Secondary stress always occurs, in polysyllabic words, on the third syllable.' The domain is the (phonological) word — 'Any Dehu (Lifu) utterance which contains no pauses and which has not more than one syllable bearing primary stress is a word' (p.1) — with no reference to root, stem or affixes.
morph.elicq: No method is stated. The only evidence presented is a list of isolated citation forms sorted by syllable count (p.2): 'EXAMPLES: Primary stress = [´], secondary stress = [`], unstress – unmarked. Words of one syllable: /kém/ father; /θín/ mother; /pí/ desire. Words of two syllables: /téðin/ brother; /séwen/ turtle ... Words of four syllables: /sínelèwen/ rainbow; /ŋáipàðø/ noon. Words of five syllables: /wátinø̀neča/ knee; /íŋaṭàpača/ sole of the foot.' The Preface states only that the monograph 'is based on linguistic material collected during fieldwork in the Loyalty Islands ... May to December 1965, and in July 1966'; the appended texts carry pause/intonation marks but no stress marks.
morph.stmt: Tryon describes Dehu as a language whose grammatical categories (tense, negation, number, definiteness, case relations, interrogation, imperative/desiderative) are carried by free particles, mostly preposed to the verb or noun ('There are no true modals in Dehu. Such ideas are translated by ordinary time markers', p.46; the four-page 'Word Level Analysis', ch.4, is the whole of the bound morphology). Bound morphology is derivational and predominantly circumfixal — 'Causative Verb: +Prefix (a) + Verb Stem + Suffix (-n)', verbaliser a-…-n, nominaliser e-…-n, reciprocal i-…-keu — plus a few prefixes (collective i-, noun-forming hna-, verbaliser ñi-, restricted reciprocal i-) and a few…

88.outw: descriptions conflict: Tryon 1968 states fixed word-initial stress (word-demarcative), Torres & Fletcher 2022 find no acoustic evidence for word stress and propose phrasal right-edge marking

Thus with the word /punepun/ perfume, the constituents are /pun/, linking vowel /e/, plus /pun/.

88.cfw: Lenormand 1954 and Tryon 1968 both describe a fixed, demarcative stress on the first syllable of the word, but the acoustic studies of Torres, Fletcher and Wigglesworth 2018, Torres and Fletcher 2020 and Torres and Fletcher 2022 find no durational or pitch cue on word-initial syllables and propose instead a phrasal right-edge prominence system, so whether Drehu has word stress at all is an open question.

89.dq: Stress patterning is predictable, and is regulated by three factors: (a) All words contain stress groups consisting of two or three syllables, of which only the initial syllable carries stress; (b) Morpheme boundaries between roots of reduplicated and compound stems affect the patterning; (c) The initial syllable of a word carries primary stress.
89.dloc: Wood 1978, Some Yuulngu Phonological Patterns (PL A-51), §3.1 p.85; StressTyp2 entry 'Gaalpu', paraphrase 'One two and three syllable words all have initial main stress and no secondary stress. Words of more than 3 syllables have a secondary stress on the penult or antepenult.'
89.prule: Primary stress word-initial; the word parses exhaustively left-to-right into stress groups of 2-3 syllables, each stressed group-initially (secondary after the first group). Per-length grids (simple words): 2=10, 3=100, 4=1010, 5=10010 (always 'sss"ss, "never the reverse", p.87 s3.5), 6=100100 (only 'sss"sss, p.86 s3.3; corrected from 100010), 7=1010010 (corrected from 1000010; Caveat: Wood p.87 s3.6 says seven-syllable secondary is hard to place — third or fourth syllable or evenly on both, i.e. 1010010 ~ 1001010 ~ 1011010; 1010010 is the pattern he actually prints in s3.4 and first in s3.6), 8=10100100 (corrected from 10000010; two printed examples, p.86). Morpheme boundaries in reduplicated/compound stems (and the bases of njiina/taaya derivatives) restart the grouping (p.86 s3.4), yielding e.g. 1100 at 4, 10100 at 5, 101010 at 6 in such words. Exceptions (p.87 s3.6): "mainly pronominals" with secondary suppressed, plus pu.'ralku, pur.'wu, pur.'wu.mi, pa.'dak ~ 'pa.dak with non-initial or variable primary.
89.srule: Secondary stress on the initial syllable of every stress group after the first: words parse left to right into groups of two or three syllables, group-initial syllables stressed, later groups 'subordinate' (weaker). 1-3 syllables: no secondary ('s, 'ss, 'sss); 4 = 'ss"ss; 5 = 'sss"ss ('never the reverse'); 6 = 'sss"sss; 7 = 'ss"sss"ss, the middle secondary heard on the third or fourth syllable or evenly on both; the two printed 8-syllable words (njiina/taaya derivatives, bases restarting the pattern) = 'ss"sss"sss. In reduplicated and compound stems the root boundary restarts the grouping ('s++"sss, 'ss++"sss, 'ss++"ss, 'ss++"sss"ss, 'ss++"sss"sss). Some words, mainly pronominals, are often heard with initial stress only.
89.quote: Stress patterning is predictable, and is regulated by three factors: (a) All words contain stress groups consisting of two or three syllables, of which only the initial syllable carries stress; (b) Morpheme boundaries between roots of reduplicated and compound stems affect the patterning; (c) The initial syllable of a word carries primary stress. [...] Words of up to three syllables have one stress group each; either 's, 'ss, or 'sss [...] Four to six syllable words contain two groups each; either 'ss"ss, 'sss"ss, or 'sss"sss

morph.stmt: Wood treats Yolŋu (incl. Gaalpu/Dhaŋu) as wholly suffixing: the map legend refers to "the approximate south western boundary of the suffixing Murngic languages" (§0.2.2 p.55), and every bound morpheme in the paper -- case (-Nha, -ḻi, -Gu, -Buy), tense/mood/aspect (-na, -la, -ma, -yi, -ŋu, -ŋa), discourse clitics (-Ma FOC, -Na DEL, -ya EMPH), nominaliser (-ṉa/-ṉaṟa), reflexive (-mi), kin suffixes (-miŋu, -manjtji) and causative/verbaliser (-ku) -- is 'suffixed to independent stems' (§4.1 p.88); plurality is by stem reduplication; no prefix of any kind is recorded.

corr.head: StressTyp2's coding matches the source only in part
corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Diegueno: In words of all sizes, primary stress falls on the final syllable. In words of all sizes, there is no secondary stress. Light monosyllables do not occur.". The source gives: One stress per word, on the last full (non-/ə/) vowel of the word; if the last vowel is /ə/, or is a short vowel in absolute word-final position, stress retracts to the immediately preceding full vowel. Stress the last full (non-/ə/) vowel of the phonological word: final stress when the word ends in a full vowel or in a consonant after a full vowel; if the last vowel is /ə/, or a word-final short vowel, stress falls on the immediately preceding full vowel (Langdon 1970:19-20, sec. 120c). Morphological equivalent: stress the last vowel of the (last) root; affixes are never stressed (p. 89, sec. 310). A small residue of non-conforming words contains the juncture phoneme /+/. 90.dq: Diegueño is a strongly stressed language, but stress is not phonemic since its placement within the word is predictable. (p. 20, sec. 131) ... It contains one and only one vowel which is distinctly more prominent in loudness and pitch than any of the other vowels in the word, and is here called "stressed". (p. 19, sec. 120c, in the definition of 'The word')

90.heavy: Stressable = a 'full vowel', i.e. any vowel except /ə/; in addition, a SHORT vowel in word-final position is never stressed (so word-finally only a long vowel, or a full vowel followed by a consonant, can bear stress). /ə/ is never stressed anywhere.
90.dflt: Not stated; does not arise (every word contains a root whose last vowel is a full vowel and is stressed, sec. 310).
90.prule: One stress per word, on the last full (non-/ə/) vowel of the word; if the last vowel is /ə/, or is a short vowel in absolute word-final position, stress retracts to the immediately preceding full vowel. Examples given by structure: CVCV́·, CVCV́C, CVCV́CəC, CVCV́CəCa.
90.srule: None in the word: it contains 'one and only one vowel which is distinctly more prominent in loudness and pitch than any of the other vowels in the word' (sec. 120c); 'Every word has one stressed vowel' (sec. 310); the pretonic loudness differences of sec. 131.1 are subphonemic tendencies, not stresses. A secondary stress is reported only in one-word reduplications, on the first element's syllable corresponding to the stressed syllable of the second ('slightly more stressed than ordinary unstressed syllables', predictable, left unmarked; sec. 610), and, per Langdon 1977:240, on the first member of a compound (xàtəpá: 'coyote' < xát 'dog' + pá: 'person'), where it 'may also further reduce so as to become indistinguishable from other unstressed material'.

90.sec_quote: Reduplication resulting in one word, with concomitant loss of stress on the first element. In these cases, the syllable of the first element corresponding to the stressed syllable of the second element bears what might be called a secondary stress since it is slightly more stressed than ordinary unstressed syllables. The occurrence of this secondary stress is predictable ... and is left unmarked.

corr.detail: StressTyp2 codes initial primary stress with secondary pattern alternating from the first syllable, no final secondary stress; the description it cites states initial primary stress ('entirely predictable from the shapes of roots and suffix morphemes') but places secondary stress by morpheme shape — third vowel of a four-syllable root, first syllable of each disyllabic suffix, monosyllabic suffixes and word-final syllables unstressed — rather than by rhythmic alternation, so runs of unstressed syllables occur (karnanhimatha 10010 beside karnawarangu 10100). The catalog follows the source.

91.dloc: Austin 2021 (2nd ed. of Austin 1981, A Grammar of Diyari), §2.5 p. 41
91.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of every phonological word (Austin 2021 sec. 2.1 p. 27; = the first vowel of the root, Diyari being entirely suffixing, sec. 1.1 p. 14; each half of a reduplicated stem is a separate phonological word with its own primary stress, sec. 2.4.3). Secondary stress on the third vowel of a four-syllable root and on the first syllable of each disyllabic suffix; monosyllabic suffixes are unstressed ('this can result in sequences of unstressed syllables'); word-final syllables are never stressed (sec. 2.5 p. 41). Secondary placement therefore follows morpheme shape, not syllable count (5-syllable karnawarangu [ˈkʌɳʌˌwɒɽʌŋu] vs karnanhimatha [ˈkʌɳʌṉiˌmʌṯʌ], Table 2.4); the grid records primary stress only, which is initial in every form of Table 2.4 (2-7 syllables). The three vowel-initial interjections arru, ayi, a'ayi are lexically initial-stressed (sec. 3.1.6 p. 47).
91.srule: Secondary stress on the third vowel of a four-syllable root; each disyllabic suffix morpheme takes (secondary) stress on its first syllable (monosyllabic suffixes unstressed; 'this can result in sequences of unstressed syllables'); word-final syllables never stressed — secondary placement follows morpheme shape, not syllable count (Austin 2021 §2.5 p. 41, Table 2.4).
91.quote: Stress in Diyari is not phonologically contrastive and is entirely predictable from the shapes of roots and suffix morphemes. Primary stress falls on the first vowel of a root and secondary stress is assigned to the third vowel of a four syllable root (no roots are longer than four syllables). Disyllabic suffix morphemes are assigned (secondary) stress on their first syllable; this can result in sequences of unstressed syllables. Note that word-final syllables are never stress in Diyari. Examples are given in Table 2.4.

Disyllabic suffix morphemes are assigned (secondary) stress on their first syllable; this can result in sequences of unstressed syllables. Note that word-final syllables are never stress[ed] in Diyari. ... Word stress in Diyari shows that morphological structure can define the domain for stress assignment."…
morph.elicq: The stress section (§2.5) gives no statement of how stress was observed. The general data statement (§1, p. 25) is: "The data upon which this study is based consist of two types of material. Firstly, sentences and vocabulary were systematically elicited by asking consultants to translate English sentences or words into Diyari and Thirari. Other material is made up of monolingual texts, including monologues ... and conversations." §2.6 (p. 42) separately contrasts "fast fluent speech such as that characteristic of texts" with forms heard "when Diyari is dictated slowly word for word", but does not tie the stress description to either.
morph.stmt: §1.1 p. 14: "Diyari is an entirely suffixing language with fairly complex nominal and verbal morphology." Word templates: "nominal word = root (-DERIVATION)n - INFLECTION" (§3.2 p. 47) and "main verb root (-DERIVATION)-INFLECTION (auxiliary)" (§3.5.9 p. 89), with up to three post-inflectional suffixes after the inflection (§4.12 p. 181).

94.dq: Normal primary stress in items of more than one syllable is on the penultimate vowel. This applies also if the vowel is member of a diphthong. Secondary stress is normally on the vowel preceding the antepenultimate. (Chadwick 1975:9)
94.dloc: the StressTyp2 entry (quoting Chadwick 1975:9); Pensalfini 2003 sec. 2.3.1 p. 36 ("The generalisations in this section apply to monomorphemic words only"), sec. 2.3.2 p. 38 ("stress is assigned to whole words (stems plus suffixes) whilst paying attention to morpheme boundaries"), sec. 2.3.1 p. 38 (variation "from utterance to utterance")
94.prule: No quantity-insensitive primary-stress rule can be stated. Per Pensalfini 2003:36-38 (monomorphemic words, counted in SBUs = vowel morae; main stress only): 2-SBU 10; 3-SBU 010 as the dictionary default against a "major lexical class" of 100; 4-SBU 0010 default with a dictionary-marked 0100 class; 5-SBU no default (00010 vs 00100 "almost evenly divided", every word listed in the dictionary); 6-SBU 000100 preferred, others listed; no monomorphemic words of 7 or more SBUs. StressTyp2's penultimate coding "10 010 0010 00010 000010 0000010 00000010" is wrong at 5 (no default), contradicted at 6 (antepenult preferred, not penult) and vacuous at 7-8.
94.srule: Monomorphemic words of four or more SBUs (vowels) carry a secondary stress on the initial SBU: 4-SBU words penult main + initial secondary (a dictionary-marked class has a single antepenult stress and no secondary); 5-SBU words always initial secondary, main penult or antepenult by word; 6-SBU words initial secondary, antepenult main preferred. Penult-stressed 3-SBU words have no initial secondary (the initial prominence is pitch). In suffixed words poly-SBU suffixes and suffix sequences are stressed on their first SBU and the rightmost stress of the word is primary, the rest secondary.

morph.rootq: "3.1 STRESS. Stress, often manifested by length, is found on the first syllable of the word. As such, it is not emic." (McAllister & McAllister 1991:134). The domain named is the word; root/stem and affixes are not mentioned. Editor's consultant note (Hartzler, p.142): "A change in this position was forced when an across-the-board first syllable stress analysis was adopted. ... Further investigation, in fact, may well reveal factors which will either disprove the stress rule, or give clues to the assimilation of these apparently paradoxical factors."
morph.elicq: The paper gives no statement of how stress was determined; the single sentence is "Stress, often manifested by length, is found on the first syllable of the word" (p.134), and every datum in the paper is an isolated citation form (phoneme-contrast and tone lists). Related remark on timing, p.135: "Doutai has word timing, that is, the same time is used for long and short words, causing short words to sound lengthened and longer words to sound jumbled." Clouse 1997:161 on the family's wordlists: "stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date."
morph.stmt: No source describes Doutai morphology as such; Clouse 1997:151 characterises the family: "all Lakes Plain languages are verb-final non-Austronesian languages. Also, a typological feature of all Lakes Plain languages is a relatively small amount of verbal affixation (isolating)", and every bound morpheme McAllister & McAllister 1991 mark (possessive -ya/-o/-edo, verbal -yake/-diwa/-wa, comitative da, p.129) follows the root, with no prefix attested anywhere in the Doutai data.

96.sec_rule: Further stresses on odd-numbered non-final syllables (Dixon's 'preferred' pattern: first and all odd-numbered syllables stressed, final syllable never). In polymorphemic words the first syllable of each root and affix is stressed, an affix-initial syllable losing its stress immediately after a stressed syllable or word-finally (pínaymárinu, núdildáriman, bánagaymbárinu). Dixon finds no phonetic evidence for two degrees of stress: non-initial stresses are not distinguished from the initial one in strength.

sources.text: Siegl 2013: 102 (sec. 2.11): "Stress is fixed and the main stress falls on the first syllable; therefore it does not need to be marked separately. morph.rootq: §2.11 Stress, p.102: "Stress is fixed and the main stress falls on the first syllable; therefore it does not need to be marked separately. Stress is realized in terms of intensity, and vowels in stressed syllables tend to be slightly longer than unstressed ones. A weak secondary stress falls on the following odd-numbered syllables." (The statement is about the word's first syllable; root/stem and suffixes are not mentioned. Since the language is exclusively suffixing, the word-initial syllable is always root-initial, but the source does not frame the rule that way.)
morph.elicq: §2.11 p.102: "Words containing more than five syllables occur seldom in either transcribed data or material from elicitation. Tereščenko (1966: 441) listed some native lexemes, which she reported as having stress on non-initial syllables, however none turned out to be stressed in this position in contemporary Forest Enets. ERRE, too, has a variety of Enets lexemes, which are marked for stress on non-initial syllables. A random test with several consultants showed that such lexemes are nevertheless stressed initially." Also fn.148: "Especially in the beginning, my fieldwork materials contain many instances where I had erroneously marked a stressed vowel as long"; and §2.5 p.95…

(§3.7 p.133); cf. §1 p.67: "Forest Enets is an entirely suffixing, mainly agglutinative language with several fusional tendencies in noun morphology... In Enggano this generally lies on the vowel of the penultimate syllable. If a word is extended by suffixes, the accent is often placed on the vowel of the penultimate syllable, but sometimes remains on the original syllable.' Cf. §11a (transl. p.18): 'Here, the accent is denoted by ′ if it rests on a vowel other than that of the penultimate syllable: euba'au my house, eubabu your house, eúbadia his house, eubaka our (incl.) house, eubáka'a …, eúbadai …, eúbadu …, eubada their house' and §11c: 'This separation of R and r by…
morph.elicq: No elicitation method is given for the accent statement. The only statement about the evidential base is the preface (transl. p.3): 'The material for the work as well as extensive texts were collected by me from July 1937 to January 1938 on the island of Enggano'; the accent passage itself moves directly from word accent to sentence intonation ('By assembling the words into sentences, they adopt certain tone sequences, the "sentence melody"') without saying whether word accent was observed in isolation or in connected speech.
morph.stmt: Old Enggano is predominantly prefixing: case/'article' markers e-, u-, i- and human plural ka- precede the noun, subject person (two prefix sets), the clause-type/voice markers bu- and ki-, causative pa-, passive di-, antipassive aN-, progressive aba-, stative/verbalising ka'a- and intensive ka- all precede the verb stem, while the suffixal inventory is small — applicatives -i and -a'a, future -a, plural -a'a, nominalisers -a/-o̲, and the possessive enclitics…

100.cfw: Kähler's 1940 grammar, the only first-hand description of pre-war Enggano, puts the accent on the penultimate syllable and Crowley (n.d.), Edwards (2015) and Hemmings & Arka (2023) all repeat him, but Yoder (2011), the one modern first-hand phonological study, finds stress consistently on the final syllable and takes the difference to be a change in the language since the 1930s.

It is not contrastive, although Key and Wyma (1964:28) considered that it has "a phonemic status [although] it also seem[s] to be predictable in some circumstances". The reason for this misinterpretation is that they missed morphological clues. The Ese Ejja accent system indeed depends highly on morphology. [...] Syllable weight does not interfe…
101.dloc: Vuillermet 2012, A grammar of Ese Ejja (Lyon 2 PhD), Ch.4 §9 p.199-200
101.prule: No single count-from-edge grid fits the source. The described rule: accent window = first three syllables of the phonological word; NOMINAL: accent on the head of the rightmost trochaic foot containing the root (surface penult for uncliticized nouns of 2-4 syllables; sigma-2 for cliticized quadrisyllabic+ nouns; overridden by intrinsically accented affixes, e.g. privative -má, and by possessive proclitics fixing sigma-3 absolutive / sigma-2 with case; e-nouns surface-final via extrametrical e-); VERBAL: accent on sigma-1, sigma-2, or sigma-3 (or word-final with RPAS =pwá) determined jointly by root syllable count x tense/mood suffix class (four arbitrary intrinsic-accent groups) x presence of -ka person indexation x stem valency (Vuillermet 2012:200-204, 224, 259-263).
101.srule: Optional binary echo of the primary accent: 'The primary accent can indeed be echoed every two other syllable, but it is not always audible' (endorsing Key & Wyma 1964:31, 'secondary stress [that] automatically falls on every other syllable in both directions from the primary stress'); in careful/elicited speech only the primary-accented syllable carries high pitch. Echoes are counted from the morphologically placed primary (sigma-1 to sigma-3), not from a word edge. Rolle & Vuillermet 2016:205-208 model them as rhythmic accents from iterative binary footing (iambic under SAG-1 suffixes, trochaic otherwise) and add no new phonetic evidence.

morph.rootq: Nominal accent, Ch.4 §9.1 p.200: 'the accent position in most cases is based on the following rules: words are divided into (disyllabic) trochaic feet; potentially accent-bearing syllables are determined from the right to the left; the possible location of the accent is limited to the first three syllables of a word; accent falls on the head of the rightmost foot that contains the root.' Also p.200: 'Ese Ejja affixes can be said to "be inherently stressed, inherently stressless, [...] remove stresses from the domain to which they are attached, assign a stress to the preceding syllable"'; e- noun prefix 'is never accented ... extrametric' (§9.3 p.203). Verbal accent, Ch.5 p.224: 'the verbal…
morph.elicq: Nominal accent (Ch.4 §9.1 p.199): 'As most word utterances given in the first subsections come from elicitation, only one pitch is associated to one syllable in each word observed.' Verbal accent (Ch.5 §2, p.227-230): 'Thousands of verb forms were collected during September 2008 in order to describe the verbal accent system ... I formed a verb with a stem + the suffix(es) chosen, and suggested the pronunciation I thought to be right; the speaker either repeated it with the same syllable accented, or corrected me ... The present study is thus based on a collection of around 2000 conjugated verb forms ... Far over 2000 forms were elicited and recorded; many have been isolated in distinct wav…
morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing and encliticising with a few prefixes/circumfixes: 'The predicate structure of inflecting verbs has a total of thirteen slots: three precede the verb root and nine follow it' (Ch.6 p.272; Ch.8 Table 35 p.366: 'The more numerous (nine) slots that follow the stem are filled by suffixes'), 'suffixes are much more frequent than prefixes in the languages' (Ch.6 §2.1.1 p.286), and 'Most grammatical morphemes are affixes or clitics, e.g. clitics for case and postpositions, suffixes for tense and mood, second-position clitics for focus and evidentials' (p.275); the prefixal material is limited to the noun prefix e-, adjectival kya-, proclitic bound possessor pronouns…

101.sec_quote: In careful speech, only the accented syllable has a high pitch [...] only one pitch is associated to one syllable in each word observed. Key and Wyma (1964:31) observed a “[predictable] secondary stress [that] automatically falls on every other syllable in both directions from the primary stress.” The primary accent can indeed be echoed every two other syllable, but it is not always audible.

101.cfw: Vuillermet's 2012 grammar and the analyses built on the same elicitation corpus by Rolle 2013 and Rolle and Vuillermet 2016, summarised by Guillaume 2023, agree that accent sits within the first three syllables of the word and is assigned by morphology rather than by syllable count or weight; the only dissent is Key and Wyma 1964, who treated stress as phonemic, and Vuillermet 2012 rejects that as having missed the morphological clues.

morph.rootq: Aralova 2015: 29-30 (§2.2.2, the basis of the 2026 sketch's phonology): 'Novikova makes it clear that it is important to distinguish between the vowels of the first syllable and the other positions in the word. The position in the first syllable is often prominent, whereas vowels in the other positions are reduced. However, in the data of the Bystraia dialect and the dialect of Sebian-Küöl, I generally observe different degrees of vowel reduction (less in Sebian-Küöl). Moreover, in my data the prominent position is not restricted to the first syllable only: the opposition is rather between the root vowels and suffix vowels. Some other factors, i.e. a long vowel in the suffix, can prevent…
morph.elicq: Aralova 2015: 62 (production study underlying her vowel description): 'Each item on the list was repeated at least three times in isolation and three times in a carrier phrase. ... The target word was in the middle position in both phrases to avoid a falling intonation pattern at the end of the phrase.' and p. 12: 'Besides these experimental data, I used a corpus of oral texts of different genres ... spontaneous narratives, conversations, pieces of folklore and procedural texts.' The prominence remark itself (pp. 29-30) is an impressionistic observation ('in my data ... I generally observe'), not an instrumental stress measurement; Pakendorf 2026's sketch is 'mainly based on the two…
morph.stmt: Pakendorf 2026: 20: 'Although Even in general has exclusively suffixal morphology, in Lamunkhin Even there is an expressive form -jakaː(n)- (glossed aug.dyn "Dynamic Augmentative") that can be synchronously analysed as infixing into the Adverbial Allative'; p. 17: 'Even is a largely agglutinative head-marking language with rich morphology... and a root-controlled vowel harmony system'; p. 27: 'a finite verb can be divided into the root (which might consist of a nominal root followed by a verbalizing suffix) and five suffix slots.' No prefixes or proclitics; the only pre-root grammatical element is the free-standing negative auxiliary ə-/e-.

102.cfw: The initial-stress coding rests on the StressTyp2 (Goedemans, Heinz and van der Hulst 2015) label, whose listed sources are Gordon (2002) and Benzing (1955, sec. 33, pp. 10-11); Benzing calls the stress "sehr unklar", places it by inference on the first syllable, and lists case endings that move it (sec. 109). Novikova (1968, 1997) describes a weak, non-phonemic stress that usually falls on the last syllable or on a long vowel, Malchukov (1995) says stress has not been experimentally studied and is not phonemic, and Cincius (1947) has no stress section in its phonetics chapter (pp. 10-44).

103.dq: 14.1. Stress. The general rule in Faroese is that stress is on the first syllable. The stressed vowels are underlined: renna 'to run', avtala 'to arrange', 'arrangement', and so on. Borrowings from Danish have the same stress pattern as in Danish (or sometimes in English)
103.dloc: Petersen & Adams 2009, Faroese: A Language Course for Beginners — Grammar, §14.1 p. 275 — (archive.org 'faroesegrammar'; opened here)
103.srule: A weak rhythmic secondary stress falls on every other syllable after the initial primary stress ('báti,num 'the boat (dat.)', 'húsi,num, 'bygdi,na, 'grinda#,hvalur); in compounds the first syllable of the second member carries the secondary stress, and this compound rule overrides the rhythmic one where they conflict ('Ís#,land, 'ís#,lendskur, 'kjallara#,búgvi). Petersen & Adams 2009 themselves state only that words have a secondary stress besides the main one (mannfólk: main stress on a, secondary on ó).
103.quote: 14.1. Stress The general rule in Faroese is that stress is on the first syllable. The stressed vowels are underlined: renna 'to run', avtala 'to arrange', 'arrangement', and so on. Borrowings from Danish have the same stress pattern as in Danish (or sometimes in English): definera 'to define', garasja 'garage', garantera 'to guarantee', and so on. [underlined in print: e of renna, initial a of avtala; e of the third syllable of definera, a of the second syllable of garasja, e of the third syllable of garantera]

morph.rootq: §14.1 Stress, p.275: "The general rule in Faroese is that stress is on the first syllable. The stressed vowels are underlined: r[e]nna 'to run', [a]vtala 'to arrange', 'arrangement', and so on. Borrowings from Danish have the same stress pattern as in Danish (or sometimes in English): defin[e]ra 'to define', gar[a]sja 'garage', garant[e]ra 'to guarantee', and so on." (brackets = underlined vowel in the print). The rule is stated over the word, not the root: the native prefixed word av-tala is shown with stress on the prefix. Only the glossary (p.292, 'Primary stress (høvuðsherðing): The main stress on a word: v[i]nur and forh[e]rðaður') implicitly shows a Danish-loan prefix for- left…
morph.elicq: p.275: "The best way to learn the pronunciation of Faroese is, of course, to listen to and imitate native speakers, use the recording that accompanies this course ... Below is a brief account of the pronunciation of Faroese." No statement of the evidence (wordlist, frames, texts or measurements) on which the stress rule rests; examples are isolated citation forms with underlined vowels.
morph.stmt: "Faroese is a highly inflected language" (p.xi); all inflection the grammar describes is by endings after the root — "Suffixes appear at the end of a word. Endings are suffixes as arm (root/stem) + suffix -ur (armur)" (glossary p.293), "as in other North Germanic languages, the definite article is a suffix in Faroese" (p.15), person/tense endings and middle -st are suffixal (pp.136-137, 169) with umlaut/ablaut alternations in strong classes — while prefixes are confined to a short derivational list (aðal-, al-, allar-, endur-, er-, mis-, ný-, ov-, ovur-, ó-, tor-, van-, ør-; §12.3 p.271) and Danish-loan verb prefixes be-, er-, for- (§7.20 p.174).

tn.quote: Both insular Scandinavian languages, i.e., Faroese and Icelandic, are head-prominence intonation languages. Head-prominence languages are languages in which phrase-level prosodic prominence is marked by the phrase head using post-lexical (intonational) pitch accents associated with the head ([1], [2]). In intonation languages, fundamental frequency (f0) is used to convey meaning at a post-lexical level, to distinguish between illocution types (e.g., questions vs. statements), or to convey attitudinal or expressive meaning (e.g., surprise, anger) or information structure (e.g., focus, topic).
tn.cite: Dehé, Nicole, Moritz Jakob, Meike Rommel & Christiane Ulbrich. 2023. The intonation of declaratives, polar questions and wh-questions in two varieties of Faroese. In Oliver Niebuhr & Malin Svensson Lundmark (eds.), Proceedings of the 13th International Conference of Nordic Prosody (Nordic Prosody XIII: Applied and Multimodal Prosody Research, Sønderborg), 117-129. Warsaw: Sciendo (De Gruyter).
tn.locator: p. 117, §1 Introduction; Faroese tonal inventory stated p. 127 §4 Discussion; H*/!H* treated as one accent type p. 126
tn.note: No lexical tone: Faroese is an intonation language; pitch is post-lexical (pitch accents H*, L+H*, L* on stressed syllables, edge tones L-L%, L-H%, H-H%), with downstep of later peaks.

104.dq: Word stress for nouns, adjectives, and prepositions places the greatest degree of stress on the rightmost syllable of the word. Similarly, phrasal stress places the most prominent stress on the rightmost word in noun phrases, adjective phrases, and prepositional phrases.

qtr.text: 13. Stress. In Fordata the stress always falls on the penultimate syllable. One should not forget, however, that two adjacent vowels form two syllables, as e.g. in akaa 'what', and therefore the stress falls on the a immediately after the k, seemingly the last syllable. In one single case the stress is on the antepenultimate syllable, namely in relational nouns whose base word ends in a consonant, when they take a possessive suffix of the 1st, 2nd or 3rd person singular, e.g. soemar 'mouth'; soemaran 'his mouth', in which latter case the stress stays on oe.

105.sec_rule: Drabbe 1926 reports a weaker second stress only in possessed relational nouns with a plural possessive suffix (-dida, -mami, -bir, -rir = Marshall's -dida, -mami, -bira, -rira): the strongest stress falls on the suffix and a less strong stress stays on the root's original stressed syllable (e.g. soemaradida, waribir), for vowel- and consonant-final roots alike. No secondary stress is described for other words; Marshall 2000 (sec. 4, pp. 197-199) marks one stress per word and does not discuss secondary stress.

108.dloc: the StressTyp2 entry note 1006; StressTyp2 365-367 pdomain='phrase'; Gordon 2002 app. p.544 'Final (of phrase)'
108.heavy: Not called 'weight' by the source: the conditioning factor is vowel quality — a final syllable with any full (non-schwa) vowel takes the stress; a syllable whose vowel is schwa cannot ('schwa is never stressed'), so stress retracts to the penult. No role for vowel length or coda consonants in placement (length is a correlate/cue of stress, sec. 5.2, not a conditioner). StressTyp1 note codes this as = 'full vowels'.
108.dflt: penult when the final syllable's vowel is schwa; no further retraction described (schwa in both final and penult not discussed)
108.prule: Word-final syllable is stressed unless its vowel is schwa, in which case the penultimate syllable is stressed; schwa never bears stress (imperative enclitic le surfaces with stressed /ø/, faites-le /fEtlǿ/). Within the phonological group all but the group-final primary stress are suppressed to reduced stresses, leaving one group stress on the final syllable of the phrase; placement is 'predictable and non-distinctive', demarcative.
108.srule: No rhythmic secondary stress described: an isolated word carries one stress (final full syllable) and, in sec. 5.2, all phrase syllables but the last are said to be of roughly equal prominence. Non-final accents arise only optionally: (i) the emphatic 'accent d'insistance' reinforcing the word's FIRST syllable, often with doubling of its consonant (c'est terrible, impossible), a style said to be spreading; (ii) in colloquial speech, initial or penultimate stress within the phrase (Fónagy 1979).

evidence_works.detail: The paper measures the formants and duration of Southern French mid vowels and finds that open-mid allophones in closed syllables are lower and more central but not shorter than close-mid allophones in open syllables, so the loi de position is not vowel reduction by shortening. Its only statement on stress, made in passing, places stress on the word-final syllable, or on the penultimate before a schwa, which matches the catalog's rule for French; it adds the instrumental point that word-final vowels are longer than word-medial ones.

evidence_works.work: Smith & Joe Pater 2020, French schwa and gradient cumulativity (Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 5(1): 24, 1-33. doi:10.5334/gjgl.583)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The article's own finding is that French schwa is pronounced more often after two consonants and more often between two stressed syllables, and that the two effects reinforce each other more than additively; the stress facts it uses are taken from earlier work, not measured. It repeats the catalog's placement (stress on the last full, non-schwa syllable, at phrase level with word-final stresses inside the phrase) and adds that a word-final stress is dropped or retracted when the next syllable is stressed, with a realized schwa able to prevent the clash.

evidence_works.work: Déprez & Yeaton 2022, On the prosody of French ambiguous multiple negative sentences (Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 7(1): 1-48. doi:10.16995/glossa.5756)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The article's own experiment finds that F0 and syllable duration separate the negative-concord reading (focused subject, compressed object) from the double-negation reading (subject and object each focused) of French sentences like 'Personne n'a vu personne'; it is a study of sentence-level focus prosody, not of word stress. Its background statement that French accent is phrase-final and phrasal rather than lexical, with the AP-final syllable lengthened, agrees with the catalog's final-stress, word-and-phrase-together entry and adds nothing new about position or secondary stress.

evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)

evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: Summary from Jun & Fougeron 2000/2002 and Delais-Roussarie et al. 2015, not the authors' own data: final stress whose domain is the accentual phrase (one or more content words plus dependent function words), optional initial secondary stress, vowel length the main correlate besides pitch, pitch accents /(aL)(Hi)(L)H*/ and boundary tones, classed as intonation-only. evidence_works.detail: The paper states that French has no word-level stress and that stress falls on the last full syllable of the Accentual Phrase, which sharpens the catalog's 'word and phrase together' domain to phrase level while keeping the final-syllable position. Its measurements concern intonation, not word stress: negatively biased questions carried an extra unaccented F0 peak on the preaccentual syllable (H+!H*) while unbiased questions had a rise on the accented final syllable (H*), so French has at least two contrastive IP-final pitch accents.

variants.quote: In SF, the final syllable of the word is stressed; and and within larger phonological phrases, this word stress is subordinated to a phrasefinal or pre-pausal stress. Stress placement in SF, as a result, is predictable and non-distinctive, serving a demarcative function (indicating word or phrase-final syllables, as the case may be). ... However, if long vowels start to appear in non-final position in popular speech or in Canadian French, these long vowels will also cause changes in the perception of stress. As a consequence, we also find stress occurring in these varieties on non-final syllables, those which have been lengthened.

109.prule: Primary stress falls on the word-initial syllable in the vast majority of words; exceptions are mainly borrowings (buntàta), some adverbs (an-diugh) and day names (Didòmhnaich).
109.srule: None inside the non-compound word: 'In stressable words one stress occurs, falling on the initial syllable' (Gillies 2009: 249); 'No secondary stress occurs except in synchronic compound forms' (Morrison 2019: sec. 2). Secondary/reduced stress arises only by subordination within phrases and in compounds. Not mentioned in Nance & Ó Maolalaigh 2021 ('Tone, intonation and stress', pp. 11-12).

109.tone: The Lewis dialect (and north-west mainland dialects such as Applecross) is described as having contrastive word accents realised as pitch: monosyllables (incl. svarabhakti words) rising or level low pitch, polysyllables (incl. hiatus words) level high / falling / rising-falling pitch; southern Hebridean and other mainland dialects are not reported to use it, and younger speakers do not use it. Stress placement (word-initial) is stated independently of the word accents.

morph.rootq: Gillies 2009 p.249: 'In stressable words one stress occurs, falling on the initial syllable: for example, deisealachadh /'d´eʃaLəxəɣ/ 'preparing', atharrachaidhean /'ahəRəxiən/ 'changes'.' The domain is the (stressable) word, not the root: p.248 'simple prepositions and conjunctions, the definite article, possessive adjectives and similar ... are treated as proclitic to stress-bearing words', and for compounds 'there is an element of variability ... either initial stress with post-tonic reductions, as in banntrach ... or a stressless or de-stressed proclitic followed by the stress-bearing word, as in bana-mhoraire /bana'ɔrar´ə/'. Nance & O Maolalaigh (JIPA) likewise: 'In the vast majority…
morph.elicq: Gillies 2009 p.231: 'The variety of Scottish Gaelic described below ... is, in the last resort, a synthetic variety – in effect 'standard' Scottish Gaelic – based on the practices of the majority of active Gaelic speakers who come from the 'central' area' (no statement of how stress was elicited; examples are cited words and phrases). The JIPA illustration rests on studio recordings of one Lewis speaker ('The recordings were made onto a laptop computer in the noise-attenuated sound studio at the University of Glasgow'; word lists and 'Transcription of the recorded passage'), but its stress sentence is a general statement not tied to a measurement.
morph.stmt: Gillies 2009 describes a language whose bound morphology is overwhelmingly post-root: nominal inflection uses 'alternation between non-palatalized and palatalized quality in final consonants' and 'addition of case- or number-marking suffixes' (p.255), the verb is 'basically analytic' with its few synthetic person, tense, mood and impersonal-passive markers all suffixal (-idh, -adh, -inn, -amaid, -ar/-te/-adh; pp.268-272), and derivation (verbal nouns, agent/abstract nouns, diminutives, adjectival -ach, verbalising -ich/-ig) is suffixal (pp.276-277); pre-root material consists of unstressable proclitics -- the definite article, possessives, prepositions/aspect particles, the past marker…

tn.quote: The Lewis dialect of Gaelic, along with north-west mainland dialects such as Applecross, is described as having contrastive word accents (Borgstrøm 1940, ... Morrison 2019). Southern Hebridean and other mainland dialects are not reported to use this prosodic feature ... Ternes (2006) provides the most extensive description of the Lewis Gaelic system. In this account, word accents correspond to differences in syllabicity: monosyllabic words have a rising or level low pitch, whereas polysyllabic words have a level high pitch, falling pitch, rising–falling pitch.

qtr.text: STRESS. In Gagauz words the stress falls predominantly on the last syllable, since the majority of affixes are stressed, e.g. al-dy-lár '(they) took', oku-máa 'to read', kalabalýk 'crowd', ikinží 'second'. If the last affix in the word is unstressed, the stress falls on the preceding syllable (affixal or root), e.g. yázma 'don't write', gagaúzça 'in Gagauz', balykçýjym 'I am a fisherman', gidä́rdi '(he) went'. Unlike other Turkic languages, in Gagauz the stress in a number of words also falls on the first syllable, e.g. báža 'chimney', gáarga 'crow', génä 'again', kávak 'poplar', ... túrna 'c…

110.dq: Ударение. В гагаузских словах ударение падает преимущественно на последний слог, т.к. в большинстве своем аффиксы являются ударными, напр.: açík 'открытый', okumáa 'читать', kızkardáş 'сестра' и др. Если последний аффикс в слове неударный, то ударение падает на предшествующий слог, напр.: gagaúzça 'по-гагаузски', insánım 'я - человек', yapárdı 'он делал' и др. morph.rootq: Main rule is stated on the word, not the root: Pokrovskaja 1997 §2.1.2 p.227 'Ударение является экспираторным, падает преимущественно на последний слог.' [Stress is expiratory and falls predominantly on the last syllable.] Morphology enters only as affix-specific exceptions: §2.3.5 p.229 'Форма 2-го лица мн. числа образуется с помощью безударного афф. -(й)ын(-ыз)... Форма 3-го лица ед. числа образуется с помощью ударного афф. -сын'; §2.3.6 p.229 (predicative person affixes on nominals) 'Эти аффиксы безударны.'; Menz 2014 p.60 on -(y)ka: 'The suffix is not stressable and does not undergo vowel-harmonic changes.' morph.elicq: Pokrovskaja 1997 §2.1.2 gives only 'Ударение является экспираторным, падает преимущественно на последний слог.' with no indication of the evidence base (no wordlist, frame, text or instrumental procedure mentioned); Menz 2014 defers phonetics to Dmitrijev (1932) ('For details on Gagauz phonetics and phonology see Dmitrijev (1932)', fn. 9) and gives no stress method either.

111.quote: In Garawa primary stress (indicated in this section by ´) is always on the first syllable of the phonological word. Primary stress is manifested by loudness, high pitch and length. yámi 'eye', púnjala 'white'. Secondary stress (indicated by `) occurs on the penultimate syllable of words with four or more syllables. Secondary stress is manifested by less length and loudness than primary stress, while pitch is usually no higher than that of contiguous syllables. morph.rootq: Furby 1974 §5 p.10: 'In Garawa primary stress (indicated in this section by ˈ) is always on the first syllable of the phonological word. Primary stress is manifested by loudness, high pitch and length. ... Secondary stress ... occurs on the penultimate syllable of words with four or more syllables. ... In words of six or more syllables tertiary stress ... occurs on every second syllable preceding the secondary stress but never on the second syllable.' The domain is the phonological word (§3.1 p.7: 'A phonological word in Garawa is defined as a minimal utterance carrying one primary stress marking the nucleus and borders marked by such devices as potential pause and phonemic distribution')…
morph.elicq: Furby 1974 does not say how stress was elicited; the stress section (§5) illustrates with single citation words only (yámi 'eye', púnjala 'white', wátjimpàŋu 'armpit', ... ŋámpalàŋinmùkunjìna 'at our many'). The endnote (p.11) states: 'The material for this paper was collected ... during eighteen months residence at Borroloola between June 1968 and March 1970. ... The author is also grateful to the University of Queensland (English Department) for the use of their spectrograph, and to Charles Peck of the Summer Institute of Linguistics for reading the spectrograms.' — spectrograms were used for the paper but are not tied specifically to the stress statements.
morph.stmt: Belfrage 1992 p.1: 'Garrwa has some typical Pama-Nyungan characteristics: it is a agglutinating, dependent-marking, suffixing language, with a "split ergative" nominal case system and relatively free word order.... Garrwa also has a set of clitics encoding various tense, aspect, mood and other meanings... hosted by pronouns and verbs'; all inflection and derivation in the consulted sources is post-root (case, number, possessive and reflexive suffixes on nominals/pronouns; conjugation-class inflectional suffixes plus TAM enclitics on verbs), the sole pre-posed bound element being the optional proclitic variant ja= of the future clitic on pronouns.

evidence_works.detail: Garawa (Furby 1974) is the exemplar of a bidirectional system: initial primary stress, secondaries on alternate syllables counted from the right edge, and an initial ternary foot in odd-parity words so that no syllable is left unfooted (seven-syllable form stressed on syllables 1, 4, 6). This agrees with the entry's initial primary, penultimate secondary and alternating further stresses that never fall on the second syllable.

sources.text: "1.8 Stress and intonation. Stress in Georgian is extremely weak and has no effect on vowel quality. The stress is so weak that linguists have not been able to agree on exactly where it falls. In words of four or fewer syllables, the stress falls on either the initial syllable or the antepenultimate syllable (third from the end). In longer words, there is a double stress: on the initial syllable and on the antepenultimate." (Aronson 1990:18-19, sec. 1.8; wording identical to the Aronson 1982 quote banked in StressTyp2)

contra.head: Published descriptions disagree on where the stress falls
contra.detail: Two instrumental studies (Jun, Vicenik & Lofstedt 2007:42-43; Borise 2023:32) find word-level stress on the initial syllable and no evidence for stress on the antepenult; the catalog follows them (see the confidence note). The cited grammar (Aronson 1990:18) instead puts the stress on either the initial or the antepenultimate syllable in words of four or fewer syllables and on both in longer words, and Gordon (2002:508, fn. 23) codes antepenultimate primary stress with an initial secondary stress in words of five or more syllables (100 0100 10100 100100 1000100 10000100), taking antepenultimate stress in four-syllable words from Zhgenti (1964), not from Aronson. That reading is quoted here …

morph.elicq: Aronson 1990 sec. 1.8 p.18: 'The stress is so weak that linguists have not been able to agree on exactly where it falls.' Amiridze 2006 contains no description of word stress.

[which] may be immediately preceded by the person markers... [which] may be preceded by the preverb... 112.cfw: Two independent instrumental studies, Jun, Vicenik and Lofstedt (2007) and Borise (2023, with Borise and Zientarski 2018), find fixed initial stress cued by duration and show the antepenultimate prominence of the older textbook rule (Robins and Waterson 1952, Aronson 1990, still assumed by Skopeteas and Féry 2016) to be a phrasal pitch target, so initial stress is the likely answer even though Georgian stress is acoustically weak and the older account has not disappeared.

evidence_works.detail: The article treats fixed initial word stress in Georgian as established, cued by duration rather than pitch, with secondary stress reported on the antepenult or penult in longer words by the earlier literature it cites, which matches the catalog's fixed-initial rule and adds the phonetic correlate and the secondary-stress detail. Its own measurements show the stressed initial syllable of nouns lengthens under narrow subject focus (means 192-216 ms vs 181 ms in broad focus) but not under object focus, while focus itself is marked by boundary tones and phrasing, not pitch accents.

morph.rootq: Fortescue 1984 §3.3.2.1 'The Role of Stress', p.340: "Stress does not play any contrastive or demarcative role in West Greenlandic. There may however be an auditory impression of relative stress on heavy syllables in connection with the intonational nucleus that covers the last morae of word forms, as discussed below (i.e. when the pitch peak of the nucleus coincides with a heavy syllable). ... The basic prosodic principle is one of quantitative 'syllable weight', as first described by Kleinschmidt"; §3.5 p.355: "West Greenlandic has no phonemic stress or tone." (No mention of root or stem; prominence is tied to syllable weight and the word/phrase-final intonational nucleus.)
morph.elicq: Fortescue 1984 p.340: "See Rischel 1974, p. 91ff, for fluctuating judgments in the past on the status of stress in the language. The basic prosodic principle is one of quantitative 'syllable weight', as first described by Kleinschmidt (see Kleinschmidt 1851, p. 7ff.). ... His discussion of 'stress' can probably be reduced to the interaction of syllable weight and intonational nucleus" — the stress statement rests on cited prior descriptions, with no elicitation method stated; the only stated prosodic data procedure concerns intonation on read connected text…
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and polysynthetic: "As with all varieties of Eskimo, the language possesses an extremely rich system of recursive derivation by suffixation" (Fortescue 1984, Introduction); inflection is "the fused person/number/mood-marker occurring in final position (before any enclitics)" (p.265), "Verbal or nominal inflections follow any derivational affix... and precede any enclitic" (p.205), and the anaphoric demonstrative element ta- is "one of the only two 'prefixes' in the language" (with deictic aa-, both confined to demonstrative stems; p.143).

116.srule: Secondary stresses exist but are optional and no placement rule is given: speakers 'can pronounce and perceive one or several secondary stresses... preceding the final primary stress', often but not only in two-root compounds; shown only in three examples — pi.ˌra.pi.ˈre 'money', o.ñe.ˌmbo.pi.ˌra.pi.re.ˈve.ta 's/he will become richer', 'ai.ˌte.gui.ˈve.ma (Estigarribia 2020:39). morph.rootq: "Native Guarani lexical roots (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) always have inherent stress, in the vast majority of cases on the last vowel. ... Prefixes are always unstressed. Suffixes and phrasal enclitics can be inherently stressed or inherently unstressed. The rule for stressing words with more than one morpheme is that the last inherently stressed morpheme will carry the word's primary stress." (§2.2.2, p.36); "The primary stress of roots almost always falls on the last syllable. In words of more than one morpheme it still tends towards the end, although this depends on the presence or absence of unstressed suffixes." (§2.2.4, p.45)
morph.elicq: No elicitation method is stated for the stress description; the prosody sketch is explicitly impressionistic: "Here I will provide a rough sketch of other prosodic characteristics, which will unfortunately be largely impressionistic due to the lack of research in this area. ... Impressionistically, stressed syllables have noticeably more intensity/volume (more so than in English or Spanish) and a higher pitch than the rest of the word, but are not necessarily longer" (§2.2.4, p.45). The grammar's data overall come from online texts, naturalistic interaction, sociolinguistic interviews (Buenos Aires 2013) and an elicitation questionnaire (Asunción/Encarnación 2018) (Preface, pp.xii-xiii)…
morph.stmt: Guarani is "a concatenative language... fully concatenative" and "agglutinative" (§1.5, pp.9-10), with roots "'augmented' with morphemes to their left and right" (p.11); "the portion to the left of a predicate (where prefixes go) is smaller and better defined (morphosyntactically and prosodically) than that to the right" — person/number, voice and optative markers are prefixed, while "the remaining morphemes follow the predicate root (the suffixes and enclitics, and any other postverbal particles). The portion to the right of the predicate presents many more options" (ch.14, pp.285-287).

116.cfw: Every source from Gregores & Suárez 1967 and Ayala 1993 to Clopper & Tonhauser 2011, Estigarribia 2020, Russell 2022 and Zubizarreta 2022 puts default stress on the final syllable, but both reference grammars and both prosody articles describe unstressed suffixes such as -ta and -ma and a few non-final roots such as óga that leave word stress on the penult or antepenult, so the system is a morphologically conditioned final default rather than the exceptionless final stress the record states.

117.dq: Stress, which is characterised by higher pitch and loudness (cf. Ladefoged 1975:222ff), identifies a word as a unit in Kuku Yalanji. Clausal intonation contours, the highest point of which is the clause stress, show some variation and are the only distinguishing feature for certain types of clauses.

117.srule: Optional secondary stress only (careful, slow citation forms; 'usually omitted'; 'In normal speech, even in long words of up to eight syllables, only the first syllable is stressed'): roots, reduplicated forms and compounds of four or more syllables may have secondary stress on the third syllable (the first syllable of the second root), or on the fourth syllable for a reduplicated trisyllabic root; disyllabic suffixes may take secondary stress on their first syllable; with monosyllabic suffixes or clitics a word of more than three syllables takes penultimate secondary stress unless the penult is the last root syllable; -baja-ku is never stressed.
117.quote: Every word in Kuku Yalanji has primary stress on the first syllable, after which there is a distinct drop in pitch for disyllabic words and a more gradual drop for words of more than two syllables (see Hershberger & Pike 1970:791-792). Words with four or more syllables that are roots, reduplicated forms, or compounds, may have secondary stress on the third syllable [...] However, secondary stress is not obligatory and is usually omitted in other than careful citation forms, leaving the word with stress only on the first syllable. morph.stmt: Kuku Yalanji is almost exclusively suffixing: 'A verb root or compound stem always occurs with an inflectional suffix and can take up to two derivational suffixes between root or stem and inflection. Up to three enclitics may follow the inflected form' (§3.8.2.1 p.87); all case inflection is suffixal (§3.2.2, Table 3.1), and among nominal stem-forming affixes there are 'seven suffixes and two prefixes' (§3.2.3 p.50), the prefixes being only derivational mala- 'expert' (possibly a proclitic) and jarra- 'rather', plus the proclitic wawu- 'since' (§3.10.1).

vlen.q: There is no phonemic distinction of vowel length as in the neighbouring languages Dyabugay and Guugu Yimidhirr. Generally, vowels in Kuku Yalanji could be classified as short, with slightly longer allophones occurring in word-final position.
